title: Preserve the required quiet zone around a QR symbol
content: DENSO WAVE defines a clear margin, or quiet zone, as necessary around a QR symbol and specifies a four-module-wide margin on every side.
signals: The poster contains a QR code that readers are expected to scan.
Text, decoration, or image details approach the edge of the QR symbol.
actions: Reserve a clear quiet zone at least four QR modules wide on all four sides of the symbol.
Keep text, borders, illustrations, and decorative texture outside the quiet zone.
constraints: Do not distort, crop, recolor, cover, or invent the QR content.
This rule supports scanability; it does not by itself prove that readers will notice the QR area.

title: Maintain minimum contrast for required poster text
content: WCAG 2.2 Success Criterion 1.4.3 applies contrast requirements to text and images of text: at least 4.5:1 for normal text and at least 3:1 for large-scale text, subject to its listed exceptions.
signals: Required text is placed over a background with similar luminance.
Readers have difficulty finding or reading required information.
actions: Use a text-to-background contrast ratio of at least 4.5:1 for required normal-size text.
Use a contrast ratio of at least 3:1 for required large-scale text.
Reduce background complexity or add a stable text field when the image behind the text prevents consistent contrast.
constraints: Treat 4.5:1 and 3:1 as thresholds and do not round a lower measured value up.
Do not change mandatory wording or event facts while improving contrast.
Apply the WCAG exceptions only when their stated conditions genuinely hold.

title: Express user-defined information priority through visual hierarchy
content: Nielsen Norman Group defines clear visual hierarchy as guiding the eye toward the most important elements and identifies color and contrast, scale, and grouping as ways to create that hierarchy.
signals: The user brief identifies information with different communication priorities.
Required elements compete at similar visual strength or an important element is difficult to discover.
actions: Use scale, contrast, and grouping to make the user-designated highest-priority information easier to discover.
Reduce competing visual strength in lower-priority decoration or secondary information.
constraints: Determine importance from the user brief and communication task, not from a generic title-first assumption.
Do not change mandatory wording or event facts.
The principle suggests design mechanisms; it does not prove a specific gaze outcome without testing.

title: Use proximity to show which poster facts belong together
content: The Gestalt principle of proximity states that items close together are likely to be perceived as part of the same group, while greater spacing implies separate groups.
signals: Related facts are visually separated or mixed with unrelated information.
Readers may have difficulty determining which label, value, or supporting detail belongs to which item.
actions: Place strongly related information, such as date and time or venue and address, closer together than unrelated groups.
Use additional spacing between distinct information groups to make their boundaries easier to understand.
constraints: Do not compress text until readability or the required quiet space around other elements is harmed.
Do not group unrelated facts merely to fill empty space.

title: Use a common region when a related information group needs a stronger boundary
content: The Gestalt principle of common region states that elements within the same boundary are perceived as related and as sharing a common characteristic or function.
signals: Related elements remain difficult to interpret as one group through spacing alone.
A required action or fact group is mixed into surrounding content.
actions: Use a restrained shared background, border, or container to bind a genuinely related information group.
Keep unrelated information outside that boundary.
constraints: Do not place the entire poster inside many competing containers.
Do not use a boundary that reduces text contrast or violates the QR quiet zone.
Use common region only for elements that are actually related.

title: Do not rely on color alone to communicate required information
content: WCAG 2.2 Success Criterion 1.4.1 states that color must not be the only visual means of conveying information, indicating an action, prompting a response, or distinguishing an element.
signals: A required action, category, or distinction is communicated only through a color change.
The meaning would disappear if the poster were viewed without reliable color discrimination.
actions: Pair color with wording, shape, scale, placement, an icon, or another visible cue that preserves the meaning.
Keep required action cues understandable when color differences are unavailable.
constraints: Do not add invented event facts or unnecessary labels.
Keep the additional cue consistent with the user's requested style and hierarchy.

title: Strengthen an ignored high-priority QR area
content: A required action entrance cannot complete its task when readers do not discover it.
signals: The QR area is required by the user.
The QR area has no visit or a much lower visit count than other required AOIs.
actions: Increase the visual prominence of the QR area without changing its content.
Add a short action cue near the QR area when the user brief allows it.
Reduce nearby decorative competition and preserve clear space around the code.
constraints: Do not cover the title, key event facts, or main subject.
Do not distort, crop, recolor, or invent the QR content.
Keep the user's requested style and information priorities.

title: Reduce comprehension cost in a repeatedly revisited title
content: Long dwell time alone does not prove interest; revisits combined with confusion may indicate comprehension difficulty.
signals: The title has repeated visits or unusually long dwell time.
Confused expression signals occur while the title is viewed.
The title is dense, ambiguous, or visually difficult to separate from the background.
actions: Shorten or visually separate the title when the original wording may be edited.
Improve title-background contrast and simplify competing decoration.
Separate title and subtitle responsibilities instead of giving both equal emphasis.
constraints: Preserve mandatory wording and facts from the user brief.
Do not infer confusion from dwell time alone.
Do not make the title dominant when the user assigned another AOI higher priority.

title: Recover visibility of required time and venue information
content: Required event facts must be discoverable even when they are not the most visually dominant content.
signals: Time or venue is required for task completion.
Readers fail to visit the time-and-venue AOI or cannot answer the related task.
actions: Group time and venue into a clear information unit.
Increase text-background contrast and reduce nearby clutter.
Place the information on the expected reading path after the title or core proposition.
constraints: Do not invent or rewrite dates, times, addresses, or organizer facts.
Keep the title and user-designated primary content above this block in hierarchy unless instructed otherwise.

title: Reduce competition when the main visual suppresses required text
content: A strong main visual is useful only when it supports rather than blocks the poster's information task.
signals: The main visual receives attention while one or more required text AOIs remain unvisited.
The ignored text overlaps a visually complex or high-contrast area.
actions: Create a quieter text zone or reduce visual complexity behind required copy.
Use spacing, alignment, contrast, or scale to restore the intended hierarchy.
Preserve the main visual but reduce decorative competition around ignored information.
constraints: Do not assume that high attention to the main visual is itself a problem.
Respect the user's priority when the main visual is intentionally more important than the title.
Preserve required visual subjects and style constraints.

title: Interpret attention relative to user-defined information priority
content: Attention metrics are not meaningful without the user's communication goal and the amount of information in each region.
signals: The system is comparing attention between AOIs with different user-assigned priorities.
actions: Compare observed attention with the priority specified in the user brief.
Consider information density and task requirements before recommending a change.
Prefer changes that improve required information without overriding explicit user choices.
constraints: User requirements take precedence over generic poster heuristics.
Do not rank AOIs by dwell time alone.
Do not treat a short dwell on concise text as failure when the related task is completed.
